title: t-SNE Exaggerates Clusters, Provably
claim: The visualization's apparent cluster structure can contradict the true input structure, so embedding output cannot be trusted to reflect input clustering.
layout: 2x3 grid, columns separated by vertical lines, output plots above input matrices
description: A 2x3 grid of panels split into three columns by thin vertical lines. The top row shows t-SNE scatter plots with black dots on gray grids. The bottom row shows the matching input pairwise distance matrices as grayscale heatmaps, each with a 0 to 1 colorbar. Row labels sit at the left: 'Output t-SNE Plot' and 'Input Pairwise Distance Matrix'. Column 1: nearly uniform input distances, yet the output shows 2 tight, well-separated clusters. Column 2: input has 2 clusters plus 1 adversarial point, yet the output is one diffuse blob. Column 3: input has 2 clusters plus outliers, yet the output shows 2 salient clusters with the outliers hidden. Titles state what each input and output contains. The eye goes first to the contrasting scatter plots, then down to the block-structured matrices.
caption: Some examples of how t-SNE may misrepresent cluster information in the input dataset.
abstract: Central to the widespread use of t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) is the conviction that it produces visualizations whose structure roughly matches that of the input. To the contrary, we prove that (1) the strength of the input clustering, and (2) the extremity of outlier points, cannot be reliably inferred from the t-SNE output. We demonstrate the prevalence of these failure modes in practice as well.
